extracted.intended_audience: schoolchildren, teachers, and general readers seeking an elementary-level introduction to Philippine life, history, and government
extracted.subtask_description: An elementary/juvenile textbook-style chapter describing Philippine customs, schooling, history, government structure, and natural hazards, intended to teach American/English-reading youth about the islands. It explains local institutions, school organization, curricular subjects, and civic arrangements under U.S. rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: School calendar / term dates
rubrics_metrics.description: “school begins about the tenth of June and closes the latter part of the following March.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains timing is tied to the hottest season (March–June) and that the school year is arranged to avoid the worst weather months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barrio school structure and progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Each barrio has its own little bamboo schoolhouse where the elementary subjects are taught; as pupils advance they go to the central town school and later to the provincial school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the multi-tiered system (barrio → town → provincial), the physical character of barrio schools (bamboo schoolhouse), and the typical progression pathway for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision and teacher development
rubrics_metrics.description: All the barrio and town teachers of one district are under the charge of an older and more experienced supervisor,--in most cases an American,--who directs the work of the schools in his territory and visits the various barrios regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisor duties include regular visits, meetings with town officials to discuss school needs, and calling teachers together to consult and give instructions regarding their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government provision and management of textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: “Filipino boys and girls do not buy their own books; the government furnishes the required texts and the pupils are allowed the use of them while they are attending school. Each child gives a receipt for all the books that are issued to him, and when school is over he returns them to his teacher and the receipt is destroyed. In case he has lost a book or has badly used it, he is required to pay for it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the administrative practice for issuing, accounting for, and reclaiming school books, and the liability for loss or damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-language teaching method (oral-object association and sentence modeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginners are taught by showing an object and saying its name (children repeat), then forming simple sentences aloud such as “This is a book,” with pupils repeating and then copying sentences from the blackboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes oral repetition, object association, incremental sentence-building, blackboard presentation, and copying as the method by which pupils learn to speak, read, and write English. Notes pronunciation difficulties (e.g., short “i” and “th”).

rubrics_metrics.name: English-only instruction policy
rubrics_metrics.description: “English was the only language used in the schoolroom, and often the boys and girls spoke it among themselves for practice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States language-of-instruction policy and the immersion practice used to promote English proficiency across multiple native-language groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary-reader awarding as recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: After some weeks of work pupils who can recognize many words are given a primary reader — described as an honor of which the child is very proud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates a milestone/reward practice tied to reading achievement and personal care of textbooks (e.g., weaving a grass cover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission requirement for provincial (high) school
rubrics_metrics.description: Any boy or girl living in the province may attend the provincial (high) school after he has completed the work of the lower grades and has passed satisfactory examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the standard eligibility: completion of lower-grade work plus passing examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provincial/high-school curriculum subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses are offered in the history and government of the United States and the Philippine Islands, in literature, in grammar and composition, in mathematics, drawing, music, cooking, sewing, manual training, agriculture, and, when called for, Spanish and other subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists the broad liberal and vocational curriculum mix intended for provincial schools; implies curricular breadth including practical subjects and civics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual training practical curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual training, begun in the upper grades, included making simple things out of bamboo and coconut wood (paper cutters, ladles, dippers, spoons, cups, ash trays) and later larger items (tables, bookcases, benches, desks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies hands-on, craft-based work progression from small articles to larger useful furniture, supporting school and barrio needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music instruction and community use
rubrics_metrics.description: Music instruction (led by a teacher noted as an excellent musician) teaches songs, reading music, and singing parts correctly; musical training is used in church services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes both classroom pedagogy and practical/community application of music education; notes Filipinos' enthusiasm and aptitude for music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-tier territorial government structure under U.S. administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States kept the three divisions already worked out by the Spaniards: insular or general government, provincial government, and municipal or town government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the overall political-administrative organization that the U.S. followed when establishing civil government in the islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central executive and lawmaking bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: At the head of all is the governor-general, who is appointed by the President of the United States. He is assisted by ... the Philippine commission. The laws for the islands are made by the Congress of the United States and by this commission acting with an assembly of representatives elected by the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes appointment and legislative arrangements under U.S. sovereignty, including interplay of U.S. Congress, appointed commission, and elected assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial, monetary, postal, and customs arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: A supreme court holds sessions in Manila; the unit of money is the peso (worth half a dollar); the post office system is separate with different stamps; a custom house collects duties and taxes are laid on liquor, tobacco, and similar articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes several administrative systems (judiciary, currency, postal, customs/tax) that define the islands' public administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provincial government offices and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each province has a governor and various other officers: a Court of First Instance, an engineer to keep roads and bridges in repair, a division superintendent of schools (under the director of education at Manila), and other legal, financial, and military officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies typical provincial offices and their responsibilities for law enforcement, infrastructure, and education oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal (town) government structure and local justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The presidente corresponds to the mayor and is aided by an elected municipal council; small cases are tried before justices of the peace, and order is kept by a municipal police force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines town-level democratic institutions and local law-and-order mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health and social policies cited as measures of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The text cites establishment of free public schools, decrease in crime and disorder, almost complete prevention of cholera and smallpox, and the removal of all lepers to one island as important results of the new era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as policy outcomes/benchmarks demonstrating the aims and effects of U.S. administration — implicit criteria for judging 'improvement' in the islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-hazard preparedness indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Houses are braced with long poles to safeguard against baguios (typhoons); weather bureau at Manila sends telegraphic reports when a typhoon approaches; boats either hasten to sheltered port or put out to sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures and institutional arrangements (weather reports, structural bracing, sheltering vessels) are described as normal precautions tied to frequent cyclones.
